correctness.rationale: For odd \(B\), prime-power analysis shows \(\beta(B)\) is a power of two exactly when \(B\) is a squarefree product of Fermat primes: even exponents give an odd value \(\beta(p^e)>1\); odd \(e\ge3\) contain a geometric factor \(R\) with \(\nu_2(R)=\nu_2((e+1)/2)\) and \(R>(e+1)/2\), hence an odd divisor; at exponent one \(p-1\) must be a power of two. For \(B=\beta(2^a)\), uniqueness of binary digits forces the Fermat-index set from \(a-1\). Even \(a\ge4\) yield \(B\equiv11\pmod{16}\), while the required product is \(3\) or \(15\pmod{16}\). For odd \(a\ge3\), a first missing binary digit contradicts the Fermat product identity modulo \(2^{2^j+1}\), forcing \(a=2^k-1\). The primes \(F_1,\dots,F_4\) and the factorization \(F_5=641\cdot6700417\) leave exactly \(a\in\{1,2,3,7,15,31\}\). The finite verifier supplements the unrestricted proof.

originality.rationale: Tóth’s original 2011 preprint proves the special family \(a=2^k-1\) and poses the existence of other super-imperfect numbers. The new necessity argument eliminates every other positive exponent among powers of two. OEIS A200758 lists the same six examples and Tóth’s special-family theorem but has no universal converse for all powers of two. Direct and equivalent-statement searches in the mathematical finding index and published literature showed no covering result. This is a bounded best-knowledge conclusion, not an absolute publication-priority proof.
residual_risks: Unindexed, obscure or later equivalent classifications of super-imperfect powers of two may exist.

value.rationale: Tóth explicitly leaves open further super-imperfect numbers. The result solves the entire natural infinite powers-of-two subfamily, not a finite slice: no as-yet-unknown large exponent qualifies. It upgrades an earlier special-form theorem and matching examples to a complete classification by a structural binary-digit obstruction. The family is canonical, since powers of two are the major examples of the iteration. The proof does not purport to settle the unrestricted problem.
